text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Introduction of longer shop-opening hours goes off quietly, higher turnover only noticeable in western city centres.
- Opposition SPD says Chancellor Helmut Kohl does not want to comment on state finances.
- Bonn to correct legal errors in communist-era east German property transfers.
- German gas industry tells European Union it remains opposed to negotiated third-party access deregulation.
HANDELSBLATT
- Hungary has asked Germany to take back 380 tonnes of toxic waste.

- Former FDP economics minister Juergen Moellemann warns that FDP politicians from North Rhine-Westphalia will refuse to vote for 1997 budget unless a two percent reduction in solidarity tax for 1998 is assured.
- Share market waiting for result of U.S. presidential election and Deutsche Telekom listing.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Coalition needs time and money. 1997 budget may not be ready in time, government faces unexpected problems this week.
- Church insists on social equality.
- Central government and states dispute issue of taking back industrial chemical waste from Hungary.
- Bakers declare as a success the first Sunday they were allowed to sell fresh bread.
- Deutsche Telekom could become the biggest seller of real estate in Germany in next few years. It could sell or rent out around a third of the 15 million square metres it owns.
DIE WELT
- Kohl demands end to coalition dispute over budget.
- Head of Evangelical church in Germany warns country is at risk of social decline.
- Millions of people make the most of longer shop opening hours. Traders in large towns happy with turnover.
- Opposition SPD is considering a legal complaint about government's budget policy.
- Germans mistrust more than ever the quality of their food. They are afraid of gene-soya, mad cow disease and salmonella.
- IG Metall union provokes employers shortly before week of protests begins.
- Institute of the German Economy (IfW) says Germany falling behind in competitive factors such as labour costs, usable lifespan of machinery and corporate taxes.
- EU wants to increase charges for freight lorries with high levels of harmful emissions.
- Tax investigators looking into 70,000 bank clients.
- Rents are higher in eastern Germany than in the west.
